newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Stronger German May M3 growth surprises mkts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Stronger German May M3 growth surprises mkts.

text.p: Germany's money supply expanded at a faster pace in May, indicating solid economic growth and confounding market expectations that the Bundesbank's main policy indicator would slow down to hit its target.

Financial markets were surprised but not alarmed after the central bank on Friday said M3 money supply expanded at an annualised rate of 7.0 percent in May from the fourth quarter of 1996, up from 6.7 percent in April.
Analysts had expected M3 to slow sufficiently to reach the Bundesbank's 1997 target growth corridor of 3.5 to 6.5 percent. Forecasts ranged from 6.0 to 6.5 percent.
German bond prices initially dropped after the news but soon made good their losses.
September futures on 10-year government bonds were up 13 basis points at 101.14 in early afternoon trade after slipping to a session low of 100.85 initially.

Analysts predicted M3 would hit the target corridor in the months ahead and said the May data did nothing to change their view that the Bundesbank would not change interest rates in the foreseeable future.
"From a domestic point of view the Bundesbank has no monetary or fundamental reason to reconsider its interest rate policy," analysts at Trinkaus & Burkhardt said in a written commentary.
The Bundesbank regards M3, which comprises cash in circulation, time, sight and short-term savings deposits, as a leading indicator of inflationary trends.

Raising interest rates too soon would choke off what has been an unspectacular economic recovery this year, while an easing is equally unlikely given the bank's insistence that current levels are not obstructing economic activity, analysts said.
The Bundesbank said M3 growth in May was driven by stronger lending to the private and public sectors.
It was also fuelled by a weakening of investment in securities -- a process known as money capital formation which tends to dampen M3 growth by siphoning money out of short-term bank accounts.

Analysts said investment in securities was hit by fears of a delay to European monetary union after Bonn revealed a big estimated shortfall in tax revenue and embarked on an abortive plan to draw on Bundesbank gold reserves.
Concern about a possible further U.S. interest rate rise also hampered investment.
Analysts said the M3 data confirmed recent indications that Europe's largest economy was on track for solid growth in the second quarter of 1997.

The Bundesbank on Thursday revised up pan-German industry orders growth to 3.7 percent month-on-month from an earlier reported 3.3 percent. Meanwhile, the Ifo economic research institute reported a brightening of business sentiment in May.
